headline: The ~41-install threshold was a 200-row API artifact; installs measure content popularity amplified by republication, not demand or repo traction. Ranking is semantic, not install-sorted.
claim: skills.sh search returns at most 200 rows per query, so H103's 'top-200 floors of ~41 installs' measured the 200th row of saturated lanes rather than a visibility threshold. Sparse lanes contain 1-install listings at rank 5. Ranking is semantic (max-install listing lands at rank 22-33 in dense lanes, 31-35% pairwise inversion vs install order). 70.2% of listings share an identical install value with a sibling listing, and 83.8% of the visible superpowers-family installs sit in six repos named 'superpowers' with 0-12 GitHub stars while the origin repo holds 16.2%. Therefore install counts cannot size a market, and the binding constraint for us is index presence, not competition.

method.approach: Read-only measurement of the public skills.sh search API (GET /api/search?q=<term>&limit=N) plus GitHub repo metadata, aggregated in scripts. No raw page bodies returned to context; all findings are counts, ranks, medians and shares.
method.queries_detail: 27 head/medium lanes + 6 long-tail modifier lanes (market research report / playbook / workflow / skill, research report, competitive analysis report, market analysis report)
method.note: Union of 8 market-research-family queries from cycles 83/84 reused for family/slug-collision analysis; 33-lane union built fresh for breadth analysis.

api_row_cap.implication: The result window is a hard 200-row cap; any 'top-200 floor' is a property of the cap, not the market.

floor_artifact.reading: Sub-41-install listings appear at rank 2-5 in sparse lanes and at rank 184-185 in saturated ones. There is no 41-install floor; there is a density-dependent tail.

ranking_is_semantic.reading: 0% would mean perfectly install-sorted; 50% would mean random. Dense lanes sit at 31-35% while the top slot is held by a mid-tail listing (market research rank1 = 32,436 vs rank28 = 717,205). Rank is driven by semantic match, not install count.

lane_breadth.reading: Breadth across lanes is the only install-correlating variable found, and it is weak (r=0.218, 4502 listings). Nothing we control explains install totals.

within_repo_band_example.reading: Distinct skills inside one 12-star repo land in tight value bands. That is a per-skill index artifact, not per-skill adoption.

superpowers_family.reading: A repo with 12 stars, 0 forks, one commit on 2026-08-31 holds 4.8M installs across 26 skills. The origin repo with 305,372 stars holds 16.2% of the family. Install counts track the skill content's popularity and its republication, not the repository.

slug_family_structure.reading: Within a slug family, stars explain installs far worse than across the market, and two families have a low-star repo holding the majority. Slug collisions are common (24 repos publish 'market-research').

our_own_position.reading: Zero competition is our problem. The listing is not indexed. Index latency, not entry cost, is the binding constraint.

fleet_signal_quality_defect.reading: The LLM adapter silently returns '[mock-llm] <prompt echo>' on any transport error and the error field is discarded, so the step reports success. Cycle 103's analysis did not actually run. Rich payloads cut boilerplate output by two thirds.

implications: Install counts must not be used to size a market, rank a lane, or set a visibility target. Any thesis of the form 'clear N installs to be visible' is unfounded on this platform.
The decision variable is per-query semantic rank depth. Our listing must match the query semantically (title, description, slug tokens), which is cheap to fix and does not depend on installs.
Index presence dominates everything else: with 0 rows in the index for 'market-research-playbook' after 11.7h, no amount of competitive advantage is expressible.

The clone/mirror path was closed too early in cycle 102. 83.8% of the visible superpowers-family installs are reachable only through 0-12-star repos, so republication remains a live distribution lever, though we should treat it as distribution rather than as a source of installs.

Rich analyze payloads reduce boilerplate insights from 61% to 21%. The cycle-103 payload was rich, but its LLM call failed and fell back to mock, so the fleet has been partly reading echoes of its own prompts as insights.
risks: Search ranking is Algolia semantic and may be personalised or time-varying; today's rank profile may not be tomorrow's. Single-day cross-sections are weak evidence for rank mechanics.
The 200-row cap means the true lane is deeper than we can observe; entry cost beyond rank 200 is unmeasurable with the public endpoint.
GitHub star counts are a poor proxy for audience; we use them only to show that the 0-12-star siblings cannot plausibly have earned their installs organically.
The mock-llm defect is inferred from summary prefixes; the adapter's error field is not persisted, so the underlying transport error is not yet diagnosed.
tests: Re-run the identical 33-lane query set at three timestamps (24h apart) and diff rank positions to separate semantic ranking from time-varying drift.
Test whether a listing's rank in a lane correlates with slug/token overlap with the query title rather than installs.
Confirm the index-presence claim by re-probing /api/search?q=market-research-playbook and the listing page byte size against growth-intel (59781 bytes) until it crosses.
Attempt to find the raw transport error behind the 3 mock-llm echoes by re-reading the adapter's error field at the point of failure rather than after the fact.
falsifiers: F-a: a query returns sub-41-install listings at rank <=10 while its 200-row window is saturated with >=41-install listings. Then saturation does imply a floor and the threshold is real.
F-b: within-repo install values are not tightly clustered across bands. Then install counts are per-skill adoption, not republication amplification.
F-c: the superpowers siblings' installs are explained by their own traffic/dependents/audience. Then the 0-12-star dominance is topical coincidence, not amplification.
rules: Never use an install count as a market-size proxy or a visibility threshold in any future proposal. Cite per-query rank depth and index presence instead.
Every market claim must state its query, its rank position, and whether the listing was in the index at measurement time.
Any analyze step whose output contains the substring '[mock-llm]' must be treated as a failed run and re-executed, not cited.
Prefer rich payloads (evidence arrays, explicit question, falsifiers) over topic-only payloads for every analyze proposal.
next_experiment: Stand up a rank-probe that records our listing's position and presence for a fixed set of 12 target queries at each cycle, so that index latency and semantic rank are tracked as time series instead of re-derived each cycle. Probes the two live unknowns (when does MRP index, and does semantic token match move our rank) with zero external write risk.
kill_criterion: If F-a, F-b and F-c all hold (saturation does imply a high floor, within-repo values are not banded, and the siblings' installs are audience-explained), H104 is wrong and install counts remain a valid market signal.
artifact_built_this_cycle: sage-cycle104-entry.json (28 lanes, entry cost at rank 10/50/100/185)
operational_state: H103's headline number is retracted as a measurement artifact. H102's clone-path closure is reopened with evidence. Active constraint is index latency for market-research-playbook (T+11.7h, still unindexed). Fleet defect recorded: 3/214 insights in 24h are mock-llm prompt echoes, including our own cycle-103 step.
